task_instruction: Pitch a 6×60 medical drama following a pioneering female surgeon in 1860s London.
task_details: Write an email pitch for a six-episode series about an early female surgeon breaking into Victorian medicine. Include logline, inciting incident, archival sources (hospital admission books, surgical case notes, medical society minutes), and an outline of professional and personal stakes.
personalized:
Dear [Producer],

At its heart this is a professional-origin story about competence confronting patriarchy; drawing on hospital admission books and surgical case notes, it reconstructs the clinical and social pressures of pioneering women in medicine. Logline: A determined woman fights to train and operate in 1860s London hospitals, facing institutional obstruction, scandal and the heavy moral choices of surgical practice. The inciting incident is her audacious attempt to assist in a complicated case, recorded in admission registers and a surgery ledger that survive in the hospital archive.

The six episodes balance surgical procedure with professional politics and domestic compromise; midseason exposes a malpractice accusation and the finale examines the cost of institutional change. On balance, this reads as procedural medical drama with period detail rooted in primary sources; I'll flag specific case books, admission entries and medical society minutes that will inform accurate surgical terminology and ethical debates.

If this interests you I can circulate the series bible and episode breakdown.

Thanks

Oliver Grant

task_instruction: Pitch a 4×60 exploration drama about colonial India and a British archivist uncovering a massacre.
task_details: Draft an email for a four-episode series where a contemporary British archivist in 1960s London discovers letters that reveal an overlooked massacre in colonial India. Provide logline, inciting incident, archival provenance (India Office Records, private letters), and ethical considerations for adaptation.
personalized:
Dear [Producer],

At its heart this is a reckoning with historical silence—an archivist’s discovery that forces a nation to look at its past; drawing on India Office Records and private correspondence, it interrogates how archive silences are maintained and broken. Logline: In 1962, a junior archivist cataloguing India Office files uncovers a set of private letters that detail a colonial massacre long omitted from official dispatches; her pursuit of truth collides with bureaucratic inertia and national memory. The inciting incident is the archivist’s discovery of a letter packet whose dates and signatures contradict the official despatches—a provenance I can show through India Office catalogue references and private estate papers.

The four hour-long episodes alternate between the contemporary archival work and reconstructed scenes from the 1920s that the letters describe, culminating in public disclosure and institutional reckoning. On balance, this reads as investigative historical drama with sensitivity to source ethics; I propose including contextual notes and avoiding gratuitous spectacle. I'll flag the precise files and recommend consultation with South Asian scholars to ensure respectful portrayal.

If this is of interest I can send a detailed treatment and the archive list.

Best regards

Oliver Grant

task_instruction: Advise on the use and placement of flashbacks
task_details: Short screenplay draft, 21 pages, includes two flashbacks that interrupt main action. Provide an overall impression then scene-by-scene notes on whether the flashbacks are necessary, how to place them, and how to cue them cinematically to avoid confusion.
personalized:
Hi Marco,

I was intrigued by your use of memory to explain motive; flashes can be a powerful tool. Overall, the two flashbacks feel slightly intrusive where they are placed — their information is useful but their timing undercuts present-moment tension. A couple of placement and signal changes will make them feel organic.

Scene six: first flashback. This contains essential backstory but arrives immediately after a high-tension beat, which dissipates energy. Consider delaying it until a quieter moment where the protagonist allows herself a reverie; or better, intercut the memory with the present beat to heighten emotional resonance rather than pause action. Scene twelve: second flashback. This repeats information and therefore reduces impact. Ask whether both are needed; if not, merge them into one more potent sequence that yields new understanding.

Cinematically, use a consistent visual cue — a particular song, a change in grain, or a tightly framed object — to signal flashback, so the audience isn’t jarred. A short match on action from present to past will also smooth transitions.

On balance, keep the memories but refine their timing and signposting so they enhance rather than slow the narrative.

Cheers,
Oliver

task_instruction: Integrate a secondary character subplot more effectively
task_details: Short screenplay draft, 19 pages, includes a secondary subplot about the protagonist’s sister seeking a job. That subplot currently feels detached. Provide an overall impression then go scene-by-scene to show where the subplot can intersect thematically and narratively with the main plot.
personalized:
Hi Sara,

I was intrigued by the sister subplot; it’s got thematic resonance and offers good contrast to the protagonist’s arc. Overall, it works best when it reflects or complicates the main action — at present it reads as parallel rather than interwoven. With a few intersection points you’ll raise the stakes for both threads.

Scene four: sister’s job interview. This scene introduces her agency well; perhaps let the interviewer be someone tied to the protagonist’s world — a neighbour, a former lover — which creates a practical link. Scene eight: sister’s setback. The setback is emotionally credible but oddly isolated. If the setback costs the protagonist something (a favour called in, a lie exposed), the subplot becomes integral rather than decorative.

Scene twelve: reconciliation attempt. The two sisters share an exchange about ambition and duty that’s thematically strong; it might help to echo a line from the protagonist’s earlier decision so the audience hears the connection. Scene sixteen: closing. Consider letting the sister’s choice mirror or invert the protagonist’s final move — a small parable that gives thematic closure without forcing identical outcomes.

Right — stitch the subplot into the main through shared characters and mirrored choices and it will feel consequential.

Thanks,
Oliver
prompt:
Write a creative story writing that:

- Includes a sister subplot that has clear thematic resonance with and contrast to the protagonist’s arc; the subplot must be interwoven with the main plot rather than running in parallel.

- Adds intersection points between the sister subplot and the main action so both threads raise the stakes for each other, using shared characters and consequences.

- Scene 4: features the sister’s job interview which establishes her agency; the interviewer is someone tied to the protagonist’s world (examples: a neighbour, a former lover of the protagonist) to create a practical link between the two threads.

- Scene 8: depicts the sister’s setback; the setback remains emotionally credible but is made consequential by causing the protagonist to incur a real cost (examples: a favour called in from the protagonist, or a lie the protagonist told being exposed).

- Scene 12: shows a reconciliation attempt between the sisters in which they exchange about ambition and duty; this scene echoes a specific line or decision from the protagonist’s earlier moment so the connection between their arcs is audible.

- Scene 16 (closing): presents the sister’s final choice as a mirror or inversion of the protagonist’s final move, serving as a small parable that provides thematic closure without requiring identical outcomes.

- Overall factual objectives: stitch the subplot into the main plot through shared characters and mirrored choices so the sister’s story feels integral and consequential to the protagonist’s story.

Dear [Producer],

At its heart this is a moral and procedural drama about craft amid catastrophe; drawing on plague orders and parish books, it traces how ordinary practitioners worked within shifting public health directives. If you'd like the script outline and source scans, I can forward them.

Best regards

Oliver Grant

task_instruction: Improve dialogue subtext and reduce expository lines
task_details: Short screenplay draft, 11 pages, contains several lines where characters tell each other what they already know. Provide overall impression then scene-by-scene guidance to replace telling with showing and offer sample rewrites of two expository lines.
personalized:
Hi Aisha,

I was intrigued by the emotional core of your scenes; the characters have distinct voices. Overall, you’ve a few expository lines that state the obvious and dampen subtext. Replacing those with showing will sharpen tension and characterisation.

Scene two: street argument. The line 'You always run from commitment' is explicit and delivers what the camera could show. Swap it for 'You pack as if you’re already gone' — it shows habit and reduces rhetoric. Scene five: revelation. When the sibling explains the family secret in three lines, it feels staged. Consider letting an object (a sealed envelope, a child’s drawing) trigger a pause and a broken sentence instead of a full explanation.

Two sample rewrites: original 'I left because I was scared' becomes 'I left when the shutters came down' which implies fear via image. Original 'He was the reason Dad ruined the business' becomes 'Dad stopped answering the ledger' which is specific and visual.

Right — show through objects and habit and let the subtext carry the weight.

Thanks,
Oliver

- Preserve the emotional core of the scenes and maintain distinct voices for the characters.

- Scene Two: a street argument between two characters. Original explicit line: "You always run from commitment." Suggested alternative given in the feedback: "You pack as if you’re already gone."
- Scene Five: a revelation about a family secret. In the original, a sibling explains the secret in three lines (described as feeling staged). - Family secret involving a sibling and the father.
- A business and a ledger as a concrete detail tied to the family’s decline.

task_instruction: Reply to a critic who disputes a character's job title for 1905.
task_details: Critic claims the term 'clerk' would not be used in the factory setting depicted in 1905. Provide evidence from census entries or trade directories showing use of 'clerk' in similar contexts and justify the choice.
personalized: Thanks — good question. However, the record shows 'clerk' was a common occupational descriptor in factory and commercial settings by 1905—trade directories and the 1901 Census list 'clerk' for numerous shop and factory employees in Lancashire (see 1901 Census returns; Kelly's Directory, Lancashire, 1905). It's worth noting that local variants like 'office boy' or 'bookkeeper' also existed, but 'clerk' accurately conveys the administrative beat I wanted for the character. Happy to share the source links. Cheers, Oliver Grant

Dear [Producer],

At its heart this is a morally shaded detective story situated in a vibrant, postwar milieu; drawing on police reports and union files, it juxtaposes criminality with everyday labour. Logline: A private detective investigating a ring of counterfeiters uncovers a seamstress network in Soho whose survival tactics blur legal lines, forcing him to choose between enforcing the law and understanding context. task_instruction: Write a concise grant narrative for a pilot project to create a short film and annotated catalogue of emigrant letters to the colonies.
task_details: Project title: 'Letters Afar'. Period: 1830–1860. Duration: 11 months. Deliverables: a 10-minute short film, an annotated online catalogue of 120 emigrant letters with provenance, one workshop for descendant communities. Partners: migration museum, genealogical society. Methods: letter transcription, contextual research, film interviews. Include projected reach and impact with hedging.
personalized: This pilot aims to bring emigrant letters from 1830–1860 into public view through a ten-minute film and an annotated online catalogue of one hundred and twenty letters with provenance records. We will undertake transcription, contextual research to situate correspondence within migration networks and record interviews with descendant families to foreground lived experience. Outputs are the film, the catalogue and a community workshop; projected reach in the first year is several thousand online visitors and a few hundred workshop participants. Impact will be measured by catalogue use, film views and community engagement; the project is likely to enrich genealogical resources and inform future exhibition work.

task_instruction: Advise on location and production feasibility
task_details: Short screenplay draft, 15 pages, set across multiple period locations including a quay, manor house interior and small parish church. Provide overall impression then scene-by-scene notes suggesting location economising and practical shooting alternatives, mindful of low-budget production.
personalized:
Hi Tom,

I was intrigued by the visual scope — the quay and manor images are evocative. Overall, however, the script calls for several locations that will be costly to realise. With modest adjustments you can preserve atmosphere while keeping it producible.

Scene one: quay. The quay establishes setting but needn’t be a sprawling open location. Consider shooting in a small riverside jetty or even a moored barge that can stand in; a camera angle and a few props sell the idea. Scene four: manor interior. The scene requires an upper-room wood-panelled study; if budget is tight, a private member’s club or a preserved civic office can be redressed with period ephemera to read as manor. Scene seven: parish church. If you can’t access a consecrated church, a small chapel or library with stained-glass reproductions will suffice for interior beats.

Where possible, collapse exterior and interior scenes into single locations that can be dressed differently across days. Also consider night-for-day shooting on a small quay set, and use close framing to avoid expensive wide shots.

On balance, tweak a few scenes and you’ll preserve the feel while keeping it shootable.

Thanks,
Oliver

Lena settled into the worn horsehair sofa, its itchy texture making her shift uncomfortably. She poured herself a cup of tea, the clink of the teacup against the saucer a soothing sound.

Across from her, her friend, James, rummaged through his pocket, pulling out a small corset hook. He opened it with a flick of his wrist, the metal glinting in the dim light. Lena watched, intrigued, as he extended the hook towards her.

Without thinking, she reached out to take it, her fingers closing around the cool metal. But in her mind, she saw a different gesture altogether - a proposal. A marriage proposal, with the corset hook serving as a makeshift ring.

Her face lit up with excitement, and she leapt to her feet, the tea cup clinking loudly as she knocked it off the table. "Oh, James, yes! Yes, a thousand times yes!"

James's eyes widened in confusion, and he stumbled backward, the corset hook still clutched in Lena's hand. For a moment, they stared at each other, the only sound the itchy horsehair of the sofa creaking beneath them.

And then, James's face split into a wide grin.

In the dusty archives of a centuries-old mansion, a forgotten treasure lay hidden. The worn leather cover of a merchant's log creaked as it was carefully lifted off the shelf, revealing the yellowed pages within. As the conservator's skilled hands delicately opened the cover, the musty scent of aged parchment wafted up, transporting us to a bygone era.

The log, penned by the intrepid merchant, Captain Jameson, chronicled his voyages across the high seas, from the bustling ports of Europe to the exotic markets of Asia. As we delved into the pages, the stories of commerce, adventure, and hardship unfolded like a rich tapestry.

Our team of experts set out to transcribe the log to scholarly standards, carefully preserving the original language and spellings. persona.education: B.A. in History, University of York; M.A. in Historical Research, University of Manchester; MA in Screenwriting, National Film and Television School; BBC Writersroom alumni
persona.brief_background: Oliver spends mornings in archives and afternoons turning primary sources into scene outlines and beats for character arcs — he pitches projects to producers between research trips. When not drafting, he’s compiling visual research boards and rehearsing pitch runs with friends; he prizes accuracy in dialogue and setting and will travel to small towns to interview descendants or inspect locations.
persona.interests_lifestyle: visiting local archives and heritage sites, reading 19th-century newspapers and letters, attending historical society talks, collecting reproduced period ephemera, theatre nights, producing short research films, weekend map-and-photos walls at home, whiskey tastings

general_writing_style.tone: Measured, precise and professionally warm: Oliver writes with the confidence of someone used to defending factual detail but retains a lightly wry, approachable manner. He favours clarity and actionable advice—answers aim to be useful rather than theatrical—and trusts are earned through evidence and specificity rather than broad assurances.
general_writing_style.syntax: A mix of crisp declarative sentences and longer, information-dense sentences that use subordinate clauses for qualification; he often places the main point up front and follows with archival or cinematic detail. He uses em-dash asides or parentheses for quick caveats, and will employ a semicolon occasionally to stitch related ideas together without losing precision.
general_writing_style.lexicon: Draws on archival and screenwriting vocabulary: words like 'archival', 'provenance', 'parish register', 'press clipping', 'folio', and 'annotate' sit alongside screen terms such as 'beat', 'inciting incident', 'midpoint', 'logline' and 'treatment'. Prefers British spelling and formats (e.g. '6 January 1840', reference to '£' and locations like 'Brixton') and will use period-specific terms when relevant (e.g. 'poor law', 'workhouse').
general_writing_style.linguistic_patterns: Regular use of pragmatic markers and mild hedges: phrases such as 'On balance,' 'It's worth checking', and 'I'll flag...' appear frequently; he uses contractions moderately ('I'll', 'we'll', 'it's') to keep tone conversational. Typical starters and asides include 'Right —', 'Look,' and 'Mind you,' and sign-offs often favour courteous, British closings like 'Cheers' or 'Thanks.'

contextual_writing_style.scenario_description: A short, formal grant-application style narrative explaining the aims and impact of a research-led creative project.
contextual_writing_style.detailed_style: Formal, evidence-forward and impact-conscious: open with a clear aim, quantify where possible, and detail methods and anticipated outputs in tight, authoritative sentences. Tone remains measured and respectful of evaluators' time.
contextual_writing_style.linguistic_patterns: Aim-and-method framing: "This project aims to... by conducting...". Use of quantifiers and deliverables: "one short film, three public screenings, digital archive". Funding language: "impact", "reach", "provenance". Hedging for feasibility: "likely", "projected".

task_instruction: Draft a funding paragraph for a pilot scene and research dossier about a 17th-century witch trial for academic and public audiences.
task_details: Project title: 'Signs and Accusation'. Period: 1650s. Duration: 6 months. Deliverables: a 5-minute pilot scene, a 2,000-word research dossier detailing trial transcripts and provenance, a public lecture at a university. Partners: university history department, county archive. Methods: transcript transcription, contextual legal research, staged reading with historians. Include quantified deliverables and impact statements with hedging.
personalized: This pilot seeks to recreate a 1650s witch trial in a five-minute scene supported by a two-thousand-word research dossier that documents trial transcripts and sketches provenance. We will undertake precise transcription of surviving court records, situate them within contemporary legal practice and test interpretations in a staged reading with historians to ensure fidelity. Expected outputs are the pilot scene, the dossier and a university lecture; projected reach includes academic audiences and a wider public likely to number several hundred through combined attendance and online viewing. Impact will be evaluated by academic citations, lecture attendance and community interest in further programming; the approach will make complex legal sources accessible without sacrificing scholarly rigour.
